title: Mechanistic interpretability is the only honest evaluation
summary: An opinion piece arguing that benchmark scores have stopped predicting model behavior on tasks that matter. [[mechanistic-interpretability]] — actually reverse-engineering the circuits — is the only path to claims that aren't just narrative.
abstract: Modern frontier models pass essentially every public benchmark, but their behavior on novel inputs remains unpredictable. Benchmark scores have a saturation problem (everyone's at 95%) and a contamination problem (the test set is in the training data). The community's response — bigger and harder benchmarks — keeps the same shape: input → score → narrative. This piece argues that mechanistic interpretability work, which directly identifies the circuits that drive a model's output, is the only methodology that can produce claims about behavior that survive distribution shift. The path is harder, the publishing rhythm slower, but the alternative is generating papers that don't constrain reality.
contentIntro:
## The benchmark crisis

In 2019 a benchmark was a falsifiable claim: 'this model gets 87% on SQuAD'. In 2025, every frontier model gets 95%+ on every benchmark, and the spread between models is smaller than the spread between two evaluations of the same model on different days. We've fit the test sets we care about; pushing harder produces marginal numbers we can't tell apart.

The field's response has been to build harder benchmarks. MMLU led to MMLU-Pro led to GPQA. Each new benchmark gets saturated within 18 months. The shape of the inquiry — score in, narrative out — never changes.

This piece argues that the only honest evaluation is mechanistic: open the model, find the circuit, show what it computes. [[mechanistic-interpretability]] is the only methodology that produces falsifiable claims about model behavior on inputs we haven't yet seen.

## What you should already know

The argument depends on understanding what circuits are: see [[induction-heads]] and [[superposition]] for two well-documented findings. If those are foreign, the rest of this piece will read as hand-waving.
contentUndergrad:
## Three failure modes of the benchmark

**1. Saturation.** When everyone's at 95%, the benchmark stops measuring capability. The remaining 5% is dominated by ambiguous questions, label noise, and luck. We can't compare frontier models with this resolution.

**2. Contamination.** Test sets leak into training data. Even with hash-based dedup and contamination audits, the closest neighbor problem persists: a paraphrase of a test question might be in the training set even if the literal question isn't. This makes 'capability' indistinguishable from 'memorization within an ε-ball'.

**3. Narrative drift.** A score is meaningless without a claim. 'GPT-X scores 87% on AGIEval' becomes 'GPT-X is approaching human-level reasoning'. The score doesn't constrain the claim. Anyone can write any narrative on top of the same benchmark numbers.

The community has tried hardware fixes (private holdouts, dynamic benchmarks, human raters). They help. They don't fundamentally change the shape of the inquiry.

## What mechanistic interpretability does differently

Mech-interp doesn't ask 'how well does this model perform?'. It asks 'what is this model computing?'. The answer is a circuit: a set of attention heads + MLP neurons + their connections that, when ablated, produce a specific behavioral change.

The canonical example is induction heads ([[induction-heads]]). Anthropic showed that a specific pair of attention heads in two-layer transformers implements [A][B] ... [A] → [B] — a simple in-context learning circuit. The claim is falsifiable: ablate those heads and the behavior disappears, on every input, not just the benchmark.

This is different from 'GPT-2 medium scores X on Y'. It's a structural claim about the model's computation. It survives distribution shift because it's an architectural property, not an input-output property.

## The path is slower and that's the point

Mech-interp papers are slow. Finding one circuit takes months; understanding a full forward pass at scale is still an open problem. There's no mass-production version of the methodology. This is uncomfortable for a field that publishes at the pace of monthly benchmark cycles.

The trade-off is what the claims constrain. A benchmark score predicts the next decimal place of that benchmark. A circuit-level claim predicts behavior across an exponentially larger input space, including inputs the field hasn't yet imagined.

## What I'm not arguing

Not that benchmarks should be abandoned. They're cheap, widely understood, and useful for triage. The argument is about which methodology should be load-bearing for high-stakes claims about model capability or alignment.

Not that mech-interp is solved. [[superposition]] alone is a multi-year research program. The point is that the methodology produces claims of a different shape; that shape matters more than the current production rate.

Not that scale doesn't matter. Larger models exhibit phenomena that smaller ones don't ([[scaling-laws]]). The claim is that scale + benchmarks tells you very little about *what* a 100B-parameter model is doing differently from a 1B-parameter model — circuits do.

## What changes if this view wins

Funding shifts toward longer-horizon interpretability work. Publication norms tolerate lower volume per author. AI safety claims are required to come with mechanistic backing or are disqualified from policy weight. The benchmark industry persists for triage but loses its central position in evaluating frontier capability.

None of this is happening yet, and the incentives mostly point the other way. The argument here is that the incentives are pointed the wrong way, not that they will reverse.
contentGrad:
## A more careful framing

The argument above is glib. Tightening it: benchmarks are a *lower bound* on capability, not a measurement. They tell you the model can do X (where X is the benchmark task) under conditions matching the test distribution. They don't tell you *how* it does X, *whether* it generalizes, or *what fails* under shift. Mech-interp aims at the second set of questions; benchmarks deliberately avoid them.

The field's pathology isn't using benchmarks; it's treating benchmark scores as if they answered the second set of questions. A 95% on MMLU does not entail 'reasoning capability'; it entails 'this distribution of inputs is solvable by this model'. The leap from one to the other is a narrative move, not an empirical one.

## Where mech-interp earns its keep

Three settings where circuit-level evidence has changed expert beliefs in the last few years:

1. **Induction heads as the substrate of in-context learning.** Anthropic 2022 demonstrated that the emergence of in-context learning during training coincides with the formation of induction heads. The mechanism is now standardly cited; the claim is testable on any new model.
2. **Superposition as a rationalization for monosemanticity failure.** Models pack more concepts than dimensions in any one layer; this explains why a single neuron rarely corresponds to a clean 'feature'. [[superposition]] gives sparse autoencoders their theoretical legitimacy.
3. **Sparse autoencoder feature dictionaries.** Anthropic and OpenAI both released circuit-level decompositions of frontier models in 2024-2025. The claims are mechanistic — a feature fires for X, ablating it changes behavior in Y way — and have already informed deployment decisions.

None of those would be in the field's vocabulary if the methodology had been 'find a benchmark and measure'.

## The honest objection

Mech-interp doesn't yet scale to GPT-4-class models in any complete sense. Most published circuits are in 100M-1B parameter range, on toy tasks. Frontier evaluation can't wait for the methodology to catch up.

Fair. The response is two-fold: (a) the methodology *has* scaled meaningfully — Anthropic's Sonnet decomposition is on a frontier-class model; (b) lacking mech-interp evidence is itself a finding. If we can't yet verify a capability claim mechanically, our confidence in it should be lower than the benchmark score suggests.

This is uncomfortable. It's also accurate.

## What I'd like the reader to take away

If you read a paper claiming a model 'reasons', ask: does the claim survive ablation of any specific circuit, or only of the entire model? If the latter, the claim is a benchmark restatement, not a structural finding. The first question is the only one mechanistic interp can answer.

paperStructure.researchQuestion: Should mechanistic interpretability replace benchmark-driven evaluation as the load-bearing methodology for high-stakes capability claims?
paperStructure.discussion: Argues yes for high-stakes claims (alignment, deployment); benchmarks remain useful for triage. The shape of mech-interp claims (circuit-level, ablation-tested) constrains a much larger input space than benchmark scores.
